summary: Friedberg is cautiously positive on Google's ability to navigate the AI search transition, noting they have competitive models, existing products, and a disciplined testing culture that should enable a managed transition — though it will require cannibalizing the existing search interface.
quote: I'm pretty positive on their ability to respond to the shift if there is one underway.

summary: Chamath argues Google has the best models in many domains and significant advantages, but faces a strategic risk from ceding the new AI query bucket to OpenAI; the market will now start pricing in search share decay, and only aggressive founder-led product cannibalization can avert structural decline.
quote: The reality is that ChatGPT is running away with it. And if you look at the growth and the share that OpenAI is seeing, it's quite an incredible thing.

summary: Jason believes Google will figure out the AI transition due to deep product integration across billions of users (YouTube, Android, Docs, Calendar), a data advantage, and Sergey Brin's active re-engagement; cost cuts could massively boost earnings.
quote: They have such integration. I think Google's going to figure this out, and if they cut their team size down, the earnings are going to go massively up.

summary: Philippe Lafont sees Google facing a classic innovator's dilemma — search is ~110% of profits but under threat, while Waymo, YouTube, and Cloud are strong assets — and wonders whether it becomes the next IBM (slow grower) or successfully reinvents itself; he personally finds the stock too complicated to call right now.
quote: Is this the next IBM? You're going to stick around for a really, really long time, but you're just not going to be like a company growing as fast as you used to... Or can they completely reengineer their business?

summary: Philippe Lafont argues that AI-driven rapid change is breaking down the Mag 7's correlated dominance, signaling the end of the era where owning just those seven names was sufficient, and investors should now think about what the next cohort of dominant companies will be.
quote: I think what AI is showing is that at a time of great change... it's a little bit like the end of the Mac 7. And what we should do is almost think like, hey, what is the next?

scoreNote: Stated as the explicit investment mandate/selection thesis for Coatue's new interval fund; basket spans public and private; named private examples include SpaceX and Stripe.
summary: Philippe Lafont's stated north star for Coatue's new interval fund is to identify and build a basket of what will be the 10 largest S&P/Nasdaq companies in 10 years — a mix of current public companies that will grow larger and private companies like SpaceX and Stripe — which he calls 'the new Mag 7.'
quote: To me, the north star is, Jason, I got to build for you in 10 years the new Mag 7. That's my job... Some are already public, they're just going to get bigger, and some are private.

scoreNote: Not scored: Chamath's quote describes the structure needed to own the basket ('you need a vehicle that can straddle both') but does not use his own transaction or selection language naming the basket as his pick or trade. It's endorsement of Philippe's framework, not Chamath's own basket call.
summary: Chamath endorses and extends Philippe's framework, arguing that the optimal basket of future dominant companies is partially public and partially private (e.g. SpaceX, Stripe), and that you need a vehicle that can straddle both to own it properly.
quote: The optimal basket of the companies you'd want to own for the future, because of these rules and regulatory burdens, are partially public, partially private. And so you need a vehicle that can straddle both if you want to own it.

summary: Chamath argues OpenAI is running away with the new AI query paradigm, attracting top talent at a pace reminiscent of Facebook's peak, and is building a distinct new use case that is potentially cannibalistic to Google search.
quote: ChatGPT is running away with it. And if you look at the growth and the share that OpenAI is seeing, it's quite an incredible thing.

summary: Philippe Lafont highlights Microsoft's Q1 report showing 100 trillion AI tokens processed (50 trillion in March alone) as a major inflection point proving AI demand is going vertical, which he sees as more market-moving than tariff concerns ('tokens >> tariffs').
quote: Microsoft said that in their Q1, they processed 100 trillion tokens, 50 trillion alone in March. And so the tokens are really going basically vertical... that was a really big deal.

summary: Chamath argues that at current course — lack of IPOs, blocked M&A, and artificially suppressed returns — venture capital cannot justify its illiquidity premium and is effectively unjustifiable as an asset class unless treated quasi-philanthropically.
quote: With the lack of IPOs and with the lack of M&A, you can't justify that asset class on its own, in my opinion, unless you think about it as something that you're doing almost philanthropically.

scoreNote: Quote is spoken by Chamath paraphrasing/extending Philippe's framework; the SpaceX/Stripe basket call belongs to both but this thesis is attributed to Guest (Philippe) as originator of the framework. Chamath's version filed separately.
summary: Philippe Lafont names SpaceX as one of the premier private companies that belongs in any forward-looking basket of the world's most important companies, alongside Stripe, as part of building the 'new Mag 7.'
quote: SpaceX would be in the basket. It's private. Correct. Stripe would be in the basket. To be long some rando public company because it's public and ignore SpaceX and Stripe would just be stupid.
